gloss_terse: wander, travel, depart (of tents being moved)
gloss_readable: This verb appears only once in Isaiah, describing a tent that will not be moved or relocated. The root shares cognates across Semitic languages related to both traveling and loading pack animals, suggesting nomadic movement. In Isaiah 33:20, the prophet envisions Zion as a secure habitation whose tent-stakes will never be pulled up—using this verb to emphasize permanence by negating the idea of wandering or departure.

senses.1: The verb describes the action of traveling or journeying, particularly in the context of moving camp or relocating a dwelling. Isaiah 33:20 uses it in a negated construction to promise that Zion's 'tent will not travel'—it will remain fixed and secure, contrasting with the transient nature of nomadic life.

gloss_terse: formed objects, images, sculptural work (particularly of cherubim)
gloss_readable: This plural noun appears only in 2 Chronicles describing the cherubim in Solomon's temple. The term refers to carved or sculpted figures—literally 'things formed' or 'image-work.' The Spanish and English translations capture the sculptural nature, while some versions simply transliterate the Hebrew, perhaps uncertain of the exact type of artistic work. These were not mere decorative elements but sacred images representing angelic beings in the Most Holy Place.

senses.1: Refers to sculptured or carved figures, specifically describing the artistic technique used to create the cherubim in Solomon's temple (2 Chr 3:10). The phrase 'image work' suggests three-dimensional carved representations rather than flat reliefs or paintings.

gloss_terse: contract, shrivel, draw together (of skin clinging to bones)
gloss_readable: This verb occurs only in Lamentations' harrowing description of Jerusalem's famine victims. The root conveys the physical contraction of skin becoming tight and dried upon the bones—a visceral image of starvation's effects. Cognate languages associate the root with binding or shackling, suggesting the constraining, constricting nature of this physical deterioration. The Spanish 'pegado' (stuck, adhered) captures how the skin clings unnaturally to the skeleton.

senses.1: Describes skin shriveling and contracting tightly upon bones due to severe emaciation. In Lamentations 4:8, this verb depicts the horrific physical state of famine victims during Jerusalem's siege, their skin drawn tight and dried against their skeletal frames.

gloss_readable: This rare feminine noun appears only in Ezekiel's oracle against Pharaoh, referring to flowing blood. The context describes blood flowing from Egypt's slain army, with sufficient volume to saturate the land. The term emphasizes the liquid, flowing nature of the blood rather than blood as a static substance. French 'vague' (wave) may capture the imagery of blood flowing in waves or surges across the battlefield.

senses.1: Denotes blood in its flowing state—the outpouring or outflow of blood from violent death. Ezekiel 32:6 uses this term in prophesying judgment against Egypt, describing how the land will be saturated with the flowing blood of the slain.

gloss_terse: Zephon (son of Gad, progenitor of Zephonite clan)
gloss_readable: This personal name designates a son of Gad and founder of a clan. The name appears in two forms in Scripture: Zephon in Numbers 26:15 and Ziphion in Genesis 46:16, representing the same individual. The etymology may connect to 'gazing' or 'watching,' though this remains uncertain. The clan descended from him became known as the Zephonites, one of the family groups within the tribe of Gad that entered Canaan.

senses.1: Personal name of one of Gad's sons who became a clan founder. Numbers 26:15 lists him in the wilderness census, where his descendants are numbered as a distinct family group within Gad's tribal allotment.

gloss_terse: Zaphon (town on east bank of Jordan in Gad's territory)
gloss_readable: This place name identifies a town in the tribal territory of Gad, east of the Jordan River. Ancient sources locate it near the Jabbok river, possibly at modern Amateh. The name may share the same root as the common word for 'north,' though here it functions as a proper noun for a specific settlement. Joshua 13:27 and Judges 12:1 both reference this Transjordanian location, important in Israel's early territorial organization.

senses.1: Geographic name of a town assigned to Gad east of the Jordan. Joshua 13:27 includes it in the boundary description of Gad's inheritance, situating it in the northern part of their territory near the Jabbok.

gloss_terse: the northerner, invader from the north (possibly locusts or foreign army)
gloss_readable: This adjective, used substantively with the article, designates 'the northern one'—an invader or threat coming from the north. Joel 2:20 applies this term to what most interpreters understand as a locust swarm, though the imagery blends with that of a military invasion. The north was the traditional direction from which Mesopotamian armies approached Israel, making 'northerner' a loaded term suggesting foreign threat and judgment. The locust plague thus functions as both literal agricultural disaster and prophetic symbol.

senses.1: Refers to a destructive force coming from the north, identified in Joel 2:20 where God promises to drive away 'the northerner.' Though locusts don't typically approach from the north, the term may emphasize the foreign, threatening nature of the plague or may metaphorically describe invading armies.

gloss_terse: the Zephonite (descendant of Zephon, member of Gadite clan)
gloss_readable: This gentelic adjective identifies members of the Zephonite clan within the tribe of Gad. Used collectively with the definite article, it designates all the descendants of Zephon (or Ziphion) listed in the wilderness census. Such clan designations were crucial for land inheritance, military organization, and maintaining genealogical records. Numbers 26:15 uses this term to categorize this particular family group within Gad's broader tribal structure.

senses.1: Collective designation for members of the Zephonite clan, descendants of Gad's son Zephon. Numbers 26:15 uses this term in the census context to identify this family group for purposes of inheritance and tribal organization.

gloss_readable: This noun appears only in Lamentations describing Judah's futile watching for help during Jerusalem's siege. The term likely derives from roots meaning 'to watch' or 'look out,' suggesting either a physical watchtower or the act of watching itself. The phrase 'in our watching we watched' uses this noun alongside its verbal form, creating emphasis through repetition—they kept watching and watching, but no rescuer came. The hoped-for military ally never materialized.

senses.1: Denotes a place of watching or the activity of keeping watch, used in Lamentations 4:17 to describe Jerusalem's desperate vigil for military help. The context suggests either a watchtower from which they observed or the extended period of watchful waiting that proved futile when their expected ally failed to arrive.

gloss_terse: Ziphion (son of Gad, alternate form of Zephon)
gloss_readable: This personal name represents the same individual called Zephon in Numbers 26:15. Genesis 46:16 uses this spelling in listing Jacob's descendants who went to Egypt. Such variant spellings for the same person are common in Hebrew genealogies, often reflecting dialectical differences or scribal tradition. The individual founded one of the clans within Gad's tribe, later designated the Zephonites in the wilderness census.

senses.1: Personal name of a son of Gad, identical to Zephon but spelled differently. Genesis 46:16 uses this form in the list of Jacob's family members who migrated to Egypt, where this son would have been born or traveled with his father.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes a type of thin, flat bread or wafer. Exodus 16:31 uses it to describe the appearance of manna, comparing the divine provision to a familiar baked good. The term suggests something thin and delicate—more like a cracker or wafer than a thick loaf. This comparison helped Israel conceptualize the unfamiliar manna by reference to known baked items, emphasizing both its bread-like sustenance and its unique, delicate character.

senses.1: Refers to a thin, flat cake or wafer, used in Exodus 16:31 as a comparison point for describing manna's appearance. The simile suggests manna resembled these delicate, thin cakes, helping Israelites understand the texture and form of this miraculous food.

gloss_terse: Zophim (high place where Balaam blessed Israel)
gloss_readable: This place name means 'watchers' or 'lookouts' and designates the location where Balak brought Balaam to view Israel's camp. Numbers 23:14 identifies it as a field on top of Pisgah, providing a vantage point overlooking the Israelite encampment. The name appropriately describes a high observation point. From this 'field of the watchers,' Balaam delivered his second oracle blessing Israel instead of cursing them, frustrating Balak's purposes.

senses.1: Geographic name of an elevated location on or near Mount Pisgah where Balaam was taken to prophesy over Israel. Numbers 23:14 identifies this 'field of watchers' as the site of Balaam's second oracle, a high point offering visual access to the Israelite camp below.

gloss_terse: treasure, that which is treasured or stored up
gloss_readable: This noun appears only in Psalm 17:14 with a textual variant (Ketiv/Qere difference). It denotes treasure or stored wealth, things of value that have been laid up or hidden away. The psalm context speaks of those whose portion is in this life, whose bellies God fills with his treasure. The term emphasizes the concept of accumulation and storage—goods set aside as precious possessions. The textual variant suggests some scribal uncertainty about the original form.

senses.1: Refers to treasure or stored valuables, used in Psalm 17:14 to describe worldly wealth that fills the bellies of those whose portion is limited to this life. The term emphasizes material goods that have been accumulated and stored as valuable possessions.

gloss_readable: This Aramaic plural noun appears in Ezra's account of the temple dedication, listing the sacrificial animals offered. The term specifies male goats, distinguishing them from female goats or other livestock. Ezra 6:17 records that during the dedication ceremonies, along with bulls and rams, they offered male goats as sin offerings for all Israel. The Aramaic vocabulary in Ezra reflects the bilingual nature of the post-exilic community and the imperial context in which the temple rebuilding occurred.

senses.1: Aramaic term for male goats or he-goats, used in Ezra 6:17 in the list of animals sacrificed at the second temple's dedication. These male goats served as sin offerings, twelve in number corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel.

gloss_terse: carpet, rug (spread out for reclining); possibly watchtower
gloss_readable: This noun presents interpretive challenges, appearing only in Isaiah 21:5's vivid scene of feasting. Most modern scholars understand it as a carpet or rug laid out for dining, part of Isaiah's portrayal of Babylon's leaders feasting heedlessly before sudden destruction. The verb 'spread' accompanying it supports this reading—they spread the carpet for reclining at table. An older interpretation took it as 'watchtower' (connecting to roots of watching), but the dining context favors the carpet/rug understanding.

senses.1: Likely refers to a carpet or rug spread for dining, used in Isaiah 21:5 in the description of Babylonian leaders preparing a feast. The phrase 'spread the carpet' suggests laying out textiles for reclining at meals, part of Isaiah's ironic picture of those feasting carelessly before judgment strikes.

gloss_terse: Zaphenath-Paneah (Egyptian throne name given to Joseph)
gloss_readable: This compound name represents the Egyptian throne name Pharaoh gave Joseph when elevating him to second-in-command. Genesis 41:45 records this renaming as part of Joseph's official installation. Egyptian scholars have identified the name as meaning something like 'the god speaks and he lives' or 'the one who provides life.' Such Egyptian names for royal officials were standard practice, marking Joseph's complete integration into Egyptian court life while maintaining his Hebrew identity in the narrative. The Greek translations struggled with the Egyptian phonology, producing various approximations.

senses.1: Egyptian throne name bestowed on Joseph by Pharaoh at his elevation to vizier of Egypt. Genesis 41:45 records this naming as part of Joseph's official investiture, marking his transformation from Hebrew prisoner to Egyptian official with an Egyptian royal name meaning approximately 'God speaks and he lives.'

gloss_readable: This noun designates a poisonous snake, possibly derived from a root suggesting hissing. Isaiah 14:29 uses it in an oracle warning Philistia not to rejoice at the breaking of their oppressor's rod, for from the serpent's root will come forth something more deadly—a viper. The imagery builds from lesser to greater threat, using snake terminology to represent political dangers. The term emphasizes the venomous, deadly nature of the creature, not just any snake but specifically a dangerous one.

senses.1: Denotes a poisonous serpent or viper, used metaphorically in Isaiah 14:29 to represent escalating political danger. The prophet warns Philistia that an even more deadly threat (symbolized by this viper) will emerge from their broken oppressor, illustrating how dangers can intensify.

gloss_terse: offshoots, descendants (as shoots from a plant)
gloss_readable: This plural noun appears only in Isaiah 22:24, parallel to 'offspring' in describing descendants. The botanical imagery presents family descendants as shoots or offshoots growing from a plant. The context speaks of Eliakim as a peg on which will hang all the weight of his father's house—both the offspring and the offshoots. The paired terms emphasize completeness, covering all generations and branches of the family. This organic metaphor for genealogical relationships was natural in an agricultural society.

senses.1: Refers to descendants or family offshoots, using botanical imagery of shoots branching from a plant. Isaiah 22:24 employs this term parallel to 'offspring' to describe all the descendants of Eliakim's family who will depend on him—both direct children and more distant relatives like shoots and branches of a family tree.

gloss_readable: This noun designates a type of willow tree, possibly named from its rustling sound. Ezekiel 17:5 uses it in an allegorical vision, describing how a great eagle took a seed and planted it 'beside abundant waters, setting it like a willow.' The simile suggests a tree that thrives near water, appropriate for willows which grow along waterways. The possible onomatopoetic origin (suggesting rustling or whisking sounds) would fit the willow's characteristic of swaying and rustling in wind along riverbanks.

senses.1: Denotes a type of willow tree, used in Ezekiel 17:5 in an allegory about planting and growth. The prophet describes planting 'like a willow'—a tree naturally suited to waterside locations, using this image within the larger allegory of Zedekiah's relationship to Babylon.

gloss_readable: This verb appears only in Judges 7:3 in God's instructions to Gideon about reducing his army. The interpretation remains somewhat uncertain—the text says 'let him return and depart' from Mount Gilead. Some connect it to Aramaic words for morning, suggesting 'depart early' or 'leave at dawn.' Others propose textual emendations. The basic sense involves departure or leaving, specifically allowing fearful soldiers to leave Gideon's camp before the battle with Midian. Whatever the precise etymology, the functional meaning—permission to depart—is clear from context.

senses.1: Means to depart or leave, possibly with nuances of early morning departure. Judges 7:3 uses this verb in God's directive to let fearful men leave Gideon's army, resulting in 22,000 departing from the 32,000 who had gathered, leaving only 10,000 before God reduced the force further.

gloss_readable: This place name identifies a Canaanite city that Judah and Simeon defeated, then renamed Hormah ('destruction'). Judges 1:17 records the conquest and renaming. The original name Zephath and the new name Hormah reflect the city's fate—it was devoted to destruction. Various locations have been proposed for its identification, including sites in the Negev south of Judah. The renaming practice reflected Israel's theological understanding that this city had come under the ban of holy war.

senses.1: Name of a Canaanite city conquered by Judah and Simeon and subsequently renamed Hormah. Judges 1:17 records how after defeating this city, they devoted it to destruction and gave it a new name reflecting its fate, establishing it as an Israelite possession in the Negev region.

gloss_readable: This noun appears only in 2 Chronicles 3:15 describing architectural features of Solomon's temple. It refers to the capital—the decorated top of a pillar or column. The term may suggest plating or overlay, indicating these capitals were covered with precious metal. The two pillars before the temple (Jachin and Boaz) were impressive architectural features, and their elaborate capitals crowned these monumental columns. The detail reflects both the grandeur of temple construction and the importance of recording its specifications.

senses.1: Denotes the capital or top of a pillar, used in 2 Chronicles 3:15 describing the two great pillars that stood before Solomon's temple. These capitals were likely plated with metal and served as the crowning decorative elements atop the massive columns.

gloss_readable: This place name designates a valley near Mareshah where King Asa of Judah met the invading Ethiopian army. 2 Chronicles 14:10 locates the battle 'in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah.' Though the precise location is debated (the Septuagint translated it as 'to the north,' leading some to emend the text), it clearly identifies a geographical feature associated with Mareshah in Judah's Shephelah region. Here Asa's much smaller army won a decisive victory by trusting in the Lord.

senses.1: Geographic name of a valley near Mareshah where Asa confronted the massive Ethiopian invasion. 2 Chronicles 14:10 identifies this valley as the battle site where Judah's king cried out to the Lord and witnessed divine intervention, routing an army of a million men.

gloss_readable: This noun appears only in 2 Kings 4:42, though the word itself remains somewhat uncertain. The context describes a man bringing firstfruits to Elisha in some kind of container. Ancient versions suggest either a garment or a bag/wallet. The most plausible reading, supported by Arabic cognates, understands it as a wallet or sack—a carrying bag for provisions. The man brought twenty loaves of barley bread and fresh grain in this sack to the prophet, provision that would miraculously feed a hundred men.

senses.1: Likely refers to a bag, sack, or wallet used to carry provisions, appearing in 2 Kings 4:42 where a man brings firstfruits to Elisha in such a container. Though the term's exact meaning is debated, the context supports understanding it as a carrying bag for food items.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes flint or hard stone, appearing only in Isaiah 5:28. The prophet uses it in a simile describing the Assyrian army's readiness—their horses' hoofs are hard 'like flint.' This comparison emphasizes strength, durability, and perhaps the ability to strike sparks. Flint's hardness made it valuable for both tools and metaphorical imagery. Some suggest reading it as 'rock' more generally, but 'flint' captures the specific connotation of exceptional hardness and the capacity to endure without wearing down.

senses.1: Refers to flint or very hard stone, used in Isaiah 5:28 to compare the hardness of invading horses' hoofs. The simile emphasizes the enemy's preparedness and durability—hoofs hard as flint that won't wear down or crack even on long campaigns.

gloss_readable: This place name identifies one of the fortified cities in Naphtali's tribal allotment. Joshua 19:35 lists it among the fortified settlements assigned to this northern tribe. The name appears to be a shortened form, possibly meaning 'rock' or 'flint,' though this remains uncertain. The Greek translation rendered it 'Tyre,' but this was likely a confusion rather than indicating the famous coastal city. The actual location of Zer remains unknown, though it was clearly significant enough to be listed among Naphtali's fortified urban centers.

senses.1: Name of a fortified city in Naphtali's territory, listed in Joshua 19:35 among the fortified settlements assigned to this tribe. Though its precise location is unknown, it was apparently significant enough to warrant mention among Naphtali's defended urban centers.

gloss_readable: This verb in its Niphal form means to be scorched or burned. Ezekiel 21:3 (20:47 in English) uses it in a prophecy against the land, declaring that all faces will be scorched by fire. The context is divine judgment pictured as an unquenchable fire consuming the land from south to north. The passive voice emphasizes that this scorching happens to people—they are the recipients of burning judgment, not the agents. The imagery is vivid and terrifying, depicting comprehensive judgment that spares no one.

senses.1: In the Niphal stem, means to be scorched or burned, used in Ezekiel 20:47 where the prophet declares judgment on the land—all faces will be scorched by the divine fire of judgment that will sweep through the territory, affecting everyone from south to north.

gloss_readable: This adjective describes something scorching or burning hot. Proverbs 16:27 uses it metaphorically, comparing a worthless person's speech to 'scorching fire'—his words burn and destroy. The simile connects verbal destructiveness to the pain of burning. Just as scorching fire chars and damages whatever it touches, so malicious speech wounds and harms. The feminine form fits with 'fire,' emphasizing the burning, searing quality of both literal flames and figurative speech that burns like fire.

senses.1: Adjective meaning scorching or burning, used in Proverbs 16:27 to characterize destructive speech. The text compares the words of a worthless person to 'scorching fire,' emphasizing how harmful speech burns and wounds like literal flames searing flesh.

gloss_readable: This feminine noun designates a rival wife in a polygamous household. 1 Samuel 1:6 uses it to describe Peninnah's relationship to Hannah—she was her rival wife or co-wife. The term inherently carries connotations of tension and competition, as multiple wives competed for their husband's attention and favor, particularly regarding children. The root suggests vexing or distressing, appropriate for a relationship characterized by jealousy and rivalry. Peninnah's provocation of the childless Hannah exemplifies the painful dynamics this noun encapsulates.

senses.1: Denotes a rival wife or co-wife in polygamous marriage, used in 1 Samuel 1:6 to describe Peninnah's relationship to Hannah. The term emphasizes the competitive, adversarial nature of their relationship—Peninnah used her fertility to provoke and distress the barren Hannah, illustrating the painful rivalries common in polygamous households.

gloss_readable: This personal name identifies the mother of Jeroboam I, the first king of the northern kingdom after Solomon's united monarchy split. 1 Kings 11:26 provides this maternal reference, noting she was a widow. In ancient Israel, identifying someone through their mother was less common than through their father, making such references notable. The name itself may connect to roots suggesting affliction or leprosy, though this remains uncertain. Her widowhood and her son's rise to kingship from non-royal origins are significant details in Jeroboam's narrative.

senses.1: Name of Jeroboam I's mother, mentioned in 1 Kings 11:26. The text specifically notes she was a widow, marking her son's non-royal origins before his rebellion against Solomon and establishment of the northern kingdom of Israel.

gloss_terse: Zeror (Benjaminite ancestor of Saul, Kish's grandfather)
gloss_readable: This personal name appears in Saul's genealogy as his great-grandfather. 1 Samuel 9:1 traces Saul's lineage back through Kish (his father), Abiel, Zeror, and Becorath to Aphiah—all Benjaminites. Such genealogical details established Saul's tribal credentials and family standing within Benjamin. The name may derive from roots suggesting binding or package, though the significance is unclear. These ancestral names anchored Israel's first king within Benjamin's tribal structure, providing legitimacy and context for his selection.

senses.1: Personal name of Saul's great-grandfather in the Benjaminite lineage. 1 Samuel 9:1 includes Zeror in the genealogy that establishes Saul's tribal pedigree, tracing his family line back through several generations of Benjaminite ancestors.

gloss_readable: This personal name identifies one of the Levitical musicians appointed by David for temple worship. 1 Chronicles 25:3 lists Zeri among the sons of Jeduthun who prophesied with lyres, harps, and cymbals. The same individual appears as Izri in verse 11, reflecting variant spellings of the same name. These musicians weren't merely performers but participated in prophetic worship—using music as a vehicle for inspired praise. Zeri/Izri was assigned the third lot in the organization of temple musicians.

senses.1: Name of a Levitical musician, son of Jeduthun, listed in 1 Chronicles 25:3 among those appointed for prophetic musical ministry in the temple. Also called Izri in verse 11, he headed the third division of musicians in David's organized worship.

gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun means need or requirement. It appears only in 2 Chronicles 2:16 (2:15 in English) where Hiram of Tyre responds to Solomon's request for timber, promising to supply wood 'according to all your need.' The term emphasizes adequacy and completeness—Hiram would provide whatever amount Solomon required, not a predetermined quantity but enough to meet the full scope of the construction project. The Aramaic vocabulary reflects the international diplomatic correspondence between these kingdoms.

senses.1: Aramaic term for need or requirement, used in 2 Chronicles 2:16 where King Hiram promises Solomon he will provide timber 'according to all your need'—emphasizing that he will supply whatever quantity the temple construction requires, not merely a fixed amount but enough to meet the complete requirement.

gloss_readable: This noun designates goldsmiths or metalworkers as a collective group or guild. Nehemiah 3:31 mentions 'son of the goldsmiths'—meaning a member of the goldsmith guild. In post-exilic Jerusalem, craftsmen organized into professional guilds for economic and social purposes. This phrase indicates guild membership rather than actual biological descent. The goldsmith mentioned was helping rebuild Jerusalem's walls, showing how various trade guilds contributed to the restoration project. Such professional designations reflected the organized structure of Jerusalem's artisan community.

senses.1: Collective noun for goldsmiths as a professional guild, appearing in Nehemiah 3:31 in the phrase 'son of the goldsmiths'—meaning a member of the goldsmith guild. This designation shows how post-exilic Jerusalem's craftsmen organized into trade associations, with guild members contributing to the wall rebuilding project.

gloss_terse: distress, cause distress, be in straits
gloss_readable: This verb means to be in distress or to cause distress, appearing in Lamentations 1:20's poignant cry of personified Jerusalem. The context is intense anguish—'my stomach churns, my heart is turned within me, for I have been very rebellious.' The verb can function transitively (causing distress) or intransitively (being distressed). Here Jerusalem experiences overwhelming distress, both emotional and physical, acknowledging this suffering as consequence of rebellion. The term conveys constriction, being pressed into narrow straits with no room for relief.

senses.1: Means to be in distress or experience anguish, used in Lamentations 1:20 where personified Jerusalem cries out about her inner turmoil and suffering. The verb conveys the experience of being pressed into straits, constricted by overwhelming trouble with no escape or relief.

gloss_terse: make a rival wife, take as co-wife
gloss_readable: This denominative verb means to make someone a rival wife—to take a woman as a co-wife to another. Leviticus 18:18 uses it in prohibiting a man from marrying his wife's sister during the wife's lifetime 'to make her a rival.' The Torah recognizes the inherent conflict in such arrangements, forbidding this particular configuration even while polygamy was permitted. The verb's existence reflects the social reality of polygamous marriages and the rivalry dynamics they produced, as seen in Hannah and Peninnah's relationship.

senses.1: Denominative verb meaning to take as a rival wife or make into a co-wife, used in Leviticus 18:18 in the prohibition against marrying a wife's sister during the wife's lifetime. The verb recognizes that taking such a second wife creates a rivalry situation, and this particular family configuration is forbidden.

gloss_terse: Zererah (location in Israel, possibly textually corrupt for Zarethan)
gloss_readable: This place name appears only in Judges 7:22, describing the Midianites' flight after Gideon's victory. The text says they fled 'toward Zererah, as far as the edge of Abel-meholah.' Most scholars consider this name textually corrupt, likely originally reading 'Zarethan' (a known location) or 'Zeredah.' The Septuagint's rendering differs significantly, suggesting early textual uncertainty. Despite the uncertain reading, it clearly designates a location in the Jordan valley toward which the routed Midianite army fled.

senses.1: Likely a corrupted place name in Judges 7:22 describing the direction of the Midianites' flight after their defeat. Most scholars believe this should read Zarethan or Zeredah, both known locations in the Jordan valley. Whatever the original form, it identifies the direction of the enemy's panicked retreat.

gloss_readable: This personal name appears in 1 Chronicles 4:7 in a genealogical list of Judah's descendants. Little else is known about this individual beyond his place in the genealogy. The name itself may connect to roots suggesting splendor or brightness, though this remains uncertain. Such genealogical records preserved tribal and family connections even when individual biographical details were lost. Chronicles' extensive genealogies served to maintain Israel's sense of identity and continuity through exile and restoration.

senses.1: Personal name of a descendant of Judah listed in 1 Chronicles 4:7. Beyond his placement in this genealogy, no other information about Zereth survives, though his inclusion in Chronicles' genealogical records preserved his connection to Judah's tribal lineage.

gloss_terse: Zereth-shahar (town in Reuben's territory, possibly meaning 'splendor of dawn')
gloss_readable: This compound place name designates a town in Reuben's tribal inheritance east of the Dead Sea. Joshua 13:19 lists it among cities assigned to Reuben. The name may mean 'splendor of dawn' or 'brightness of morning,' possibly describing its location or characteristics. It has been tentatively identified with modern es-Sara on a spur of Mount Attarus. The location would have been part of the Transjordanian highlands overlooking the Dead Sea—terrain characterized by dramatic views and morning light.

senses.1: Name of a town assigned to Reuben, listed in Joshua 13:19 among their territorial cities. Possibly meaning 'splendor of dawn,' it has been identified with a site on the highlands east of the Dead Sea, part of Reuben's Transjordanian inheritance.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes vomit—what has been expelled from the stomach. Proverbs 26:11 uses it in a memorable and grotesque comparison: 'As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly.' The image is deliberately repulsive to emphasize the fool's senseless return to destructive behavior. Just as a dog's return to its vomit is nauseating and irrational, so is the fool's repetition of folly. The proverb became proverbial itself, quoted in 2 Peter 2:22 to describe false teachers returning to their former ways.

senses.1: Refers to vomit or what has been vomited, used in Proverbs 26:11 in a vivid simile about foolish behavior. The proverb compares a fool repeating his folly to a dog returning to its vomit—both are disgusting and senseless acts of returning to what should be abandoned.
